There’s more imagination in a single frame of Into the Spider-Verse than in most superhero films put together. The animation is ridiculous, the music keeps it moving, and I like how goofy it’s willing to be. I just wish the characters had been given as much attention as the world around them. Miles and Peter B. Parker have a real connection; most of the others feel like a great design followed by a punchline. I had fun watching it, but for a film that looks this inventive, the story plays things surprisingly safe

Sure he has to experience changes of becoming spider-man but he’s also gone to a new school, he’s making new friends, he’s attempting to attain a girlfriend, he has new school rules and grades to keep up with, he’s moved to a new city: you get the point. i love the action in it, i love the animation, i love the music— it gets you very involved  in the film which is definitely important yet not always achievable so they’ve done a good job. i would have just liked the action to be a little…more, if that makes sense?

I wondered if I would like this more on rewatch. When I watched this the first time, I probably had a lot of Marvel fatigue, and I liked Across the Spider-Verse a lot since. But I think this is a tough rewatch as well as a tough thing to watch after having watched... even more Marvel stuff, including Deadpool & Wolverine. I want to get the most technical problem I have out of the way, though: for as innovative and psychedelic as this animation is, I think it's hard to look at sometimes. Visually, there are just too many ideas and not all of them work. The "halftone shader"? Love it. The chromatic aberration effects? They get a little distracting sometimes. The way they render depth of field? Hate it. When they are running out of the lab through the cafeteria, there is a shot that begins only with scientists sitting at a table out of focus (because our heroes aren't in frame yet). It looks horrible. When anything is very out of focus, it looks horrible. (I don't recall having these quibbles with Across; I assume without reading my review that they ironed out the kinks of this aesthetic.) Now, not unlike the look, the story and its comedy both have moments while also having problems. My problems with the story are enormous in 2026, and it's a testament to what I do like about this movie that it gets a positive score from me. Because... if I really had to say, I would say I do not like this movie. It's just so... I'm sorry, it's just so Marvel. Self-congratulatory IP-waving? Check. Bad science fiction? Check. Unwelcome self-reflexive glibness? Check. Unrelatably high stakes? Check. I have gone from having a distaste for these qualities in Marvel stories to simply not tolerating them. I remember being bummed on my first viewing of this movie that it felt like it ended on a hamfisted "and you could be Spider-Man too, so care about him and his many revenue-generating incarnations, please" note. I completely forgot that it's way more crass up front. The early character development in this movie is not Miles Morales as Spider-Man or Peter Parker as Spider-Man or a different Peter Parker as Spider-Man. It's Spider-Man as intellectual property. And it's not like other superhero fiction hasn't done this. I know specifically of Superman and Wonder Woman fiction that acknowledges their celebrity in-world, even going so far as to include comic books of these characters (like this movie does). But the ends justify the means so much better in those stories. This just feels like Marvel reminding you of how big Spider-Man is in our world, not his own. Because the Spider-Man of this movie's (main) world is one of two people. It's Peter Parker, who died early and isn't established all that well in any real detail. Again, he and every other Spider-Man are overshadowed by Spider-Man (tm). Or, it's Miles Morales, who gets Spider-Mogged in his own movie. I just find his arc to be really unsatisfying: he's bad at Spider-Stuff until he's pretty suddenly not and... Guys, this plot is all and only about fixing and inserting a USB drive (which Sweatpants Peter himself mocks in typical Marvel movie fashion... guys, if you want to talk me into the idea that your movie is bad, don't be upset when I agree with you). Bad. Science. Fiction. And we run away from all of Miles's worldly relationships immediately in order to remedy multiversal concerns of little tangibility (though they do try to humanize Kingpin and it's more convincing than it has much right to be). Furthermore, when you blast past reality with that much impatience, I begin to have my own impatience about your inability to tell stories about heroism that have any real-life connections. We do not need superheroes to model how to act in the face of a supercollider when we've fallen on the magical thumb drive that saves the world. We need models of actual interpersonal bravery and compassion (but then again I would say that as a Wonder Woman fan), for when we're challenged with much more likely problems. Look. It has moments and a groundbreaking (if flawed) look. But, again... it's just SO Marvel. And I'm really, really tired of that tone and those problems that are so common to these stories. Next time you consume a Marvel story, I want you to try something. Ask "what if I didn't care about the most extremely made-up parts of this?" I think it makes these stories fall apart really often and reveals how much Marvel expects us to just buy in as a matter of course. I think you see this attitude in the way they flex Spider-Man as IP here and do an MCU victory lap around the X-Men movies (which have rich stories apart from the mutations) in Deadpool & Wolverine. This movie is about Spider-Man (tm), not Miles Morales. I wish I'd learned more about him, what he cares about, and the people who live on the same Earth as him. And I don't think these are unreasonable demands to make on a story.

Je ne suis généralement plus trop fan des films de super-héros (merci marvel), mais il faut dire que cette nouvelle saga a su attirer mon attention au vu des critiques qu'elle a suscité y compris au niveau de ceux qui ne sont pas fan de super-héros. J'ai d'abord trouvé le film très drôle, les gags sont vraiment bien amenés et pas trop lourd, que ce soit le père qui demande à son fils de lui dire "je t'aime", ou simplement les situations inconfortables dans lesquelles Miles se trouve. Le rythme assez rapide du film permet de ne pas s'ennuyer, et cela est d'autant plus appuyé vers la fin avec les différents styles d'animation proposé en fonction d'où proviennent les différents personnages. Au niveau de l'intrigue par contre c'est moins bien de manière générale, bien que je trouve le début avec la mort de Peter Parker assez réussie, la suite va vraiment être un peu trop basique à mon gout. Il y a d'abord l'antagoniste qui a mon sens n'a qu'un proto-développement un peu bâclé, des facilités un peu grossières comme la meuf spiderman qui est dans le labo et qui arrive à la rescousse, c'est assez curieux. J'ai aussi trouvé qu'il y a eu un certain manque de progressivité dans le power up de Miles, genre il passe vraiment du tout au tout sans transition, sans vraiment se découvrir. Bref, l'histoire bien que trop basique se regarde bien grâce aux touches d'humour et l'animation originale. Un bon moment.

I'm not really into Spider-Man as a franchise, I thought the Sam Rami films were fine, but apart from that I haven't been tempted to check out more films. What drew me to "Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse", is the creative and beautiful animation. I got what was expected, gorgeous animation and a decent story. Miles is an interesting character, but the rest of the characters feel weak and underdeveloped. What I didn't expect was for the film to be this funny, I was laughing through most of it, which made it more enjoyable. I thought this film was well done but I'll probably forget it in a week.
